The vaccination point belongs here. It is one of the values that would determine whether I could raise children inside a community at all. I’m not trying to design a village for everyone; communities need enough agreement on children’s health that parents can actually trust one another.

The grown child’s review matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can describe their intentions forever. The person who lived through the system may eventually describe something else.
community-s8a/u1.A:
This would be a value I would require in a community if I was going to raise children there. I am not trying to design a community for everyone, but I think that communities need to agree on certain things when it comes to the health of children.

I think that the review by the now grown child is far more important than what the founders of this village say.
community-s8a/u1.B:
This is why I think the vaccination point has to go in there. It's pretty fundamental in terms of what I would want in a community if I were to bring children into it. It's not like I'm trying to design a village for everybody but it seems to me there should be a fairly strong consensus when it comes to the health of children in a community.

I think in the long run the person who actually lived through it will give a better review than the founders.

community-s8a/u3.input:
My position is that mothers raise their own children inside a community where care is genuinely shared. The village can carry meals, supervision, teaching, protection, play, and much of fathering. It should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

Jean Liedloff’s The Continuum Concept is one of the biggest reasons I think community matters for children. Her Ye’kuana account is one outsider’s interpretation and may idealize what she saw, but the picture remains powerful: babies carried inside ordinary adult life, children surrounded by several ages, learning through participation, and one exhausted parent not expected to become the child’s whole social world. A nuclear household can imitate pieces of this. A real village can make it normal.
community-s8a/u3.A:
For the record I am entirely in favour of Mothers raising their own children, within the context of a community that helps to raise them. Not to take them away, but to help look after them, feed them, watch them, teach them, protect them, play with them, even father them to a large extent.

One of the reasons that I want children to grow up within a community, is due to the book "The Continuum Concept" by Jean Liedloff. Even accepting that what she describes about the Ye'kuana people may be coloured by her own perspective and that she is romanticising them, there is still a lot about the way that they raise their children that is very beneficial. Especially the way that the babies are integrated into adult life and the multi-generational approach to raising children. While it is possible to mimic this to an extent within a nuclear household environment, it is much better if done within the context of a real village.
community-s8a/u3.B:
I'm arguing here for mothers raising their own children but in a healthy community structure where "the village" helps to raise the child. Not to take the child away from the mother to "liberate" her but to do all the many things that go into child rearing (meals, watching, teaching, protecting, playing, etc, etc) even including much of what is called fathering.

One of the benefits of a community structure for children has been delineated by Jean Liedloff in her book "The Continuum Concept". Her observations of the Ye'kuana tribe are obviously colored by her viewpoint and no doubt she romanticized things a bit, but her ideas of how to bring up children in a way that incorporates them into adult life, has multi-age groups all around them, etc, etc are very valuable and can be done somewhat in a "nuclear" family setting but would be infinitely better in a "village" setting.

community-s8a/u4.input:
Experiments with children sleeping and living separately from parents deserve special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that communal sleeping eventually ended through a mixture of developmental findings, parental preferences, and social change. High-quality group care and multiple loving adults can benefit children; replacing secure parental attachment is a different proposition.

Tamera’s Children’s Place deserves direct study rather than caricature. My own bias remains with systems that expand a child’s circle without making the parent-child bond ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8a/u4.A:
That’s a fascinating experiment, but one that would be dangerous to try out with children. A similar idea was tried at the Israeli Kibbutzim for a while (kids sleeping and living separately from their parents), but eventually abandoned due to…well, read the link to find out why. That said, high quality group care with many loving adults is great for kids, but doesn’t replace secure attachment with parents.

In the meantime, check out Tamera’s Children’s Place…

Personally, and biasedly, the systems that work best for kids are those that can supplement the parent-child relationship without being ideologically opposed to it.
community-s8a/u4.B:
This is something that would need to be experimented with very carefully. The Israeli kibbutzim tried something similar, but eventually gave it up for a variety of reasons. That said, it is possible that it could work under the right circumstances - there is certainly a lot to be said for children being able to experience high quality care in a group setting, with multiple loving adults to care for them. But it can't be a substitute for secure attachment with parents.

In the case of Tamera's Children's Place, it would be interesting to check it out for myself. But personally, it's biased toward a system that doesn't regard the parent-child relationship as something that should be ideologically subordinated to other concerns.

community-s8a/u5.input:
Children also need territory that belongs to them—places where they can develop a society of children, create games, resolve ordinary disputes, and experience some freedom from constant adult management.

I tasted that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it remains one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG’s Kinderhaus works from a similar intuition. Adults hold the outer safety. Children still get a world.
community-s8a/u5.A:
Yes, children also need their own space where they can develop their own society and play games.

I do remember from one Unitarian youth camp a very free experience. And here in the Kinderhaus of ZEGG adults make sure, that outside children are safe, but inside of this they can develop their own world.
community-s8a/u5.B:
Children need their own territories to form their own society and invent their own games.

I have one of the most free memories of my life from a Unitarian youth camp. That's why I am really excited about what the ZEGG Kinderhaus is doing, too. The adults are there to make sure it's safe on the outside.

community-s8a/u6.input:
This can be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards need to be explicit. A children’s territory cannot become a place where adults stop paying attention, where older children quietly dominate younger ones, or where secrecy is treated as independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats every warm relationship between an unrelated adult and child as suspicious. Children benefit from many adults who know them, enjoy them, notice changes, and will act when something is wrong. Fear can destroy that gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8a/u6.A:
I realise it can be taken the wrong way so just to clarify there will be safeguards in place. This will not be a territory where the adults are unaware of what is happening or where older children lord it over younger children or where it is kept a secret from the adults.

I am also not one of those suburbanites who sees wrong in any relationship between a child and an adult who is not related to them. Children need to have relationships with lots of adults who like them and who would act if anything was amiss. It’s the fear that really sucks.
community-s8a/u6.B:
This is so easy to misconstrue, I feel like I have to add caveats: This does not mean it's okay for adults to give their children a territory where the adults are not welcome, where older children can terrorize younger children, or keep secrets.

Also, I don't think it's helpful (and this is coming from a suburban mom) to act like it's weird or suspect for children to have warm relationships with adults who aren't related to them. It's great for kids to have a bunch of adults who like them, know them, and will stick up for them if necessary.

community-s8a/u7.input:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. Their “no” matters. Adults aren’t entitled to affection, physical contact, obedience outside legitimate safety needs, or private access.

Create a no-secrets rule. No adult asks a child to hide a gift, game, touch, conversation, or relationship from the child’s mother or another trusted adult. Surprises have an ending date. Secrets designed to isolate the child are forbidden.
community-s8a/u7.A:
The parts of this protection are:

- Teaching them they have power, that they have a voice, and that they can say no to adults. Adults are not owed their love, physical contact, obedience, if not for legitimate safety needs, or access to them.

- No secrets. No adult may tell them to keep something from their mother or other trusted adults. No adult can give them a gift, play a game, touch them, talk about things, or form any kind of relationship with them that they can not then talk about with their mother or other trusted adult. There can be a surprise, because the surprise will end on a certain date, but there can not be a secret that serves to keep them isolated from the trusted adults in their life.
community-s8a/u7.B:
A few of the things to do to protect them are:

Teach them that they have control over their bodies and that “No” is a complete sentence. They do not need to show anyone affection or let anyone touch them if they do not want to, unless it is an absolute, legitimate necessity. They do not have to obey anyone, nor does anyone get to be allowed into their private space, unless it is an absolute necessity to keep them safe.

Have a strict “No Secrets” policy. No one is allowed to tell them not to tell their Mom (or other trusted adult) about a gift, game, touching, conversation, relationship, etc. that they have with another person. Surprises are different, because there is a time at which the surprise will be revealed. But secrets that serve to separate them from their Mom or trusted adult are not allowed.

community-s8a/u8.input:
Teach truthfulness before a crisis. Children should understand that their words carry power and that adults will listen seriously. This education must never become interrogation, punishment for uncertainty, or a reason to dismiss a report. A frightened or confused child may tell a story imperfectly and still need protection.

Hear the child even when the accused person is beloved. Communities fail here because the adult may be charismatic, useful, wealthy, spiritually important, or everybody’s friend. Decide the response process before anyone’s face is attached to it. Immediate safety comes first; investigation must be competent and fair; nobody’s status buys silence.
community-s8a/u8.A:
This suggests at least two points. One is the importance of teaching children the value of telling the truth, the power of their words, and ensuring that they know their words will be taken seriously. This teaching should never be done in a way that is interrogative or that would in any way punish children for not being able to tell the truth. Even when a child is not able to tell the story in a perfect way, the first need is to take action to protect that child.

The other point is that adults must learn to listen to the words of children even when those words accuse someone whom the adults love. Too often, communities fail to do this because the accused person is charismatic, or important in some way, or well-off, or an important spiritual leader, or a good friend to people in the community. It is important to have a process that will be followed when a child accuses someone of abuse. This process needs to be put in place before the face of a particular person is put on the situation. The process should be aimed at providing immediate safety for the child, and should include a process for fair and competent investigation of the accusation.
community-s8a/u8.B:
Teach children the importance of telling the truth and how seriously their words will be taken, without making them feel that they may be punished for not being able to explain things well enough.

Listen to them when they tell on someone that the community loves. Prepare the community to do the same thing by having a pre-determined process for how to respond to accusations of child sexual abuse. Often the alleged perpetrator is charismatic and seems to be so helpful. The community must be prepared in advance to do the right thing (i.e. make sure the children are safe, and have a good investigation) even if the person being accused is wealthy, a spiritual leader, or someone that everyone likes.

community-s8a/u9.input: Keep relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, and other trusted adults give children perspective and somewhere to speak. At least one trusted adult, advocate, or reporting route should be reachable without going through community leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children during the Island Pond raid, and the court returned them after rejecting the state’s blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. Total community enclosure can also fail. Children need more than one world.
community-s8a/u9.A: Make sure that they have relationships and reporting route outside the community. Whether these are grandparents, cousins, friends in a nearby community, teachers or other trusted adults, it is important for the children to have perspective on their life and to have someone to talk to if needed. Make sure they have at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route that doesn’t go directly to the leadership of the community. Remember, the state has tried this before, in 1984, when authorities raided Island Pond, Vermont, and seized 112 children. The state’s blanket request to take the children was rejected by a court and the children were returned. Trying to enclose these children completely within a community can also fail. Let the children have more than one world.
community-s8a/u9.B: Make sure that there are relationships and ways to report problems that are outside of the community: grand-parents, cousins, “regular” friends, teachers, etc. Children need to have context and ways to report that don’t go through the community. Make sure they have at least one person they can go to for help, at least one person who will be on their side, and at least one way for them to report abuse that doesn’t go to the leaders of the community. Remember, in 1984, the State of Vermont raided Island Pond and took 112 children. A court subsequently threw out the State’s blanket request to take the children and sent them back. The State may not be able to help, but at least they’re another set of eyes on the community. Enclosing the children totally within the community doesn’t work. They need to experience other worlds.

community-s8a/u10.input: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented intentional-community case in which a child remained seriously dangerous to other people and the record followed the whole sequence: conduct, assessment, intervention, review, and what happened later. I did not find one. That may be because records are private or cases were routed elsewhere, but it means I cannot claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version internally. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community does not control.
community-s8a/u10.A: There's another reason I feel that this problem cannot be effectively dealt with within the context of a particular intentional community. I searched through my relatively large corpus of stored research material for an actual case from an intentional community (where all the details are known) in which a child had become seriously dangerous to people and the entire sequence of events, assessments, interventions, and long term outcomes are known. And I found nothing. It's quite possible that... Always ensure that the child, the family, and the endangered people have access to competent help and review processes that are not controlled by the home community.
community-s8a/u10.B: I have searched through this corpus of information on ICs and I don't believe that there is a single instance that is well-documented where the entire process and its aftermath is described for a serious case involving a child who is seriously dangerous to other people. Therefore I don't believe that there is any collective experience with how to deal with such a case internally within a community. For this reason alone, it is essential that the child, the family, and the potential victims have access to competent help and review that is not under the control of the home community.

community-s8a/u11.input:
Amish youth make an adult choice about whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. The popular caricature of Rumspringa as a universal teenage free-for-all is exaggerated, but adult baptism still matters: belonging becomes a commitment rather than a fact imposed at birth.

A community whose children never leave cannot know whether they would freely return. Let them study, travel, make friends, encounter other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8a/u11.A:
This is not a choice made by youths, but by adults, and 85% or more do become members. The Rumspringa thing is blown out of proportion, but the fact that they are not included until they choose to be baptized as adults is significant.

If the children of a given society never leave it, how do the leaders of that society know that the children would voluntarily choose to stay? Allow the children to see the rest of the world. Allow them to study, to travel, to be friends with, to be in disagreement with the founders of their community, and not be looked on as traitors for doing so.
community-s8a/u11.B:
It's not a choice made by youth, though, it's made by adults. While the Rumspringa is blown way out of proportion, it's true that the youth are allowed to be wild-children. But 85%, or more, choose to join the church when they are old enough to make that decision. It matters, because they are baptized as adults, not as children.

If they never leave, how will they ever know they wanted to join it? Let them learn, let them travel, let them make friends, let them be against the foundors.

community-s8a/u12.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary families do not hand an eighteen-year-old a pile of money to go explore the world; they try to prepare them for some viable next step. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care, and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8a/u12.A: This all depends on their upbringing, if they grew up poor and around a no money community than most likely they do n't have the funds to even provide for basic necessities like food or medical care and stuff like that. But even if they grew up in a normal community parents do n't usually just give their kid a bunch of money at eighteen, they most likely are helping them prepare for something viable.
community-s8a/u12.B: Its quite likely no matter where a person was raised if they are born into a community that is poor or has no money. No matter what community a person is born into few parents will give an 18 year old money to travel. Most parents want to make sure the person has some form of viable future. In communities that are poor the focus is more on survival of the person, food, medical care, etc.

community-s8a/u13.input: The realistic standard is not unlimited freedom. It is that leaving should not be made artificially impossible. If children grow up without using money, they especially need enough knowledge of the outside money world not to be helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, identification, transportation, and how to ask for help. They need portable skills and education, relationships beyond the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next path—school, apprenticeship, work, family, or another community. If the community can offer temporary housing, travel help, tools, or a small transition reserve, great. If it cannot, it can still avoid punishing departure or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function elsewhere. No upbringing offers perfect freedom. The point is not to erase path dependence; it is not to turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8a/u13.A: What is more realistically possible, and still meets the spirit of that standard, is that it not be artificially impossible for a child to leave a community. This will require, especially for children raised without exposure to money, that they be educated on the nature of money to the point that they are not helpless in a money based world. To the extent possible this will also require that they be educated and skilled in a way that is not dependent on that specific community, that they have at least some relations outside the community, that they have access to their records and documents, and that they at least have some obvious next step to take. Ideally the community would assist with this transition, but if not the least they can do is not make it harder than it already is, and not prevent the above mentioned things from happening. While perfect freedom from path dependance is impossible to attain, it is possible to not make it artificially impossible.
community-s8a/u13.B: A more realistic standard might be that the community should not try to make it artificially impossible for their children to leave. This might mean educating them more thoroughly about how the outside money-world works, especially if they aren't exposed to money in their daily lives. It might also mean teaching them skills and education that are more portable outside the community, encouraging them to have outside relationships, helping them to obtain records and documents, and being sure that they have some idea of where they could go next. If the community has the resources, it could also provide transition assistance, like temporary housing, transportation, tools, or even a transition reserve. But even if they don't, they can at least avoid doing things that punish people for leaving or make it harder for them to function in the outside world. Perfect freedom may not be possible, but there are things a community can do to avoid creating path dependence.

community-s8a/u14.input:
Some may leave permanently; others may start communities with different values rather than waiting decades to inherit the original version. Parents may experience that as loss even when the movement is evolving.

Couples who share a home, culture, and bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline, and medical care. Multiply that by twenty adults with twenty childhoods.

Goodwill doesn’t answer those questions after a child is already living inside the disagreement. Communities need enough shared child-rearing principles to offer coherence, plus enough room for parents to remain parents.
community-s8a/u14.A:
Some might even leave and set up a community with more like-minded people, rather than waiting for what they want to trickle down over decades. Which would, of course, be devastating for the parents.

Couples living in the same house, sharing the same culture and sleeping in the same bed, often separate because they can’t agree about screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline, medical care, etc. And that’s with only two people and two childhoods to draw on, not twenty and twenty.

Goodwill isn’t enough. There needs to be some sort of common ground when it comes to how to raise a child; but there also needs to be space for the parents.
community-s8a/u14.B:
That may mean some leaving and staying away, some starting new communities to get their vision of child rearing instead of waiting 20+ years for theirs to come to fruition. At the least, it’s going to feel like a loss to some parents.

Couples that live together, eat together, share a culture, sleep in the same bed, still split apart over issues like screen time, vaccines, schooling, religion, diet, discipline, medical care, etc. Imagine adding 19 more adults into the mix with 20 different childhoods.

There has to be a mix of “What if the child is already there?” and “everyone needs to come to the table with good will” in every community or it won’t have the shared coherence necessary for a healthy community AND it won’t allow for the parents to be parents.

Once my children are grown, I'll write a review.

My position is that mothers raise their own children, inside a community where the care really is shared. The village can take on meals, supervision, teaching, protection, play, and a lot of the fathering. It should never take a child away from the mother in the name of liberating her.

Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept is one of the biggest reasons I think community matters for children. Her account of the Ye'kuana is one outsider's interpretation, and she may idealize what she saw. But the picture is still powerful. Babies are carried inside ordinary adult life. Children are surrounded by people of several ages, and they learn by taking part. And one exhausted parent isn't expected to become the child's whole social world. A nuclear household can imitate pieces of this. A real village can make it normal.
community-s8b/u3.A:
I say Mothers should be permitted to raise their own children within a community where the village raises the child in regards to everything except removing the child from it's Mother. The village should help with feeding, watching, teaching, protecting, playing with, and even fathering of the child but not remove the child from it's Mother in order to liberate the Mother from the child.

One of the reasons I say that children need a community to help raise them comes from the book Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff. Although it is just an interpretation by an outsider and may be an idealization of the Ye'kuana tribe, she does show some very good aspects of raising children in a tribe. Some of them include the baby being carried with him all the time and being included in adult activity, having multi-age groups for the children to interact with, inclusion of the child in activity, and not relying on one tired out parent to be the sole social influence on a child. Some of these can be mimicked by the nuclear house hold but a true village would benefit the child much more.
community-s8b/u3.B:
Well, my view is that mothers should raise their children, but with the help of the village. The village does NOT raise the children instead of the mother, but they help out with things like feeding the child, watching him, teaching him, protecting him, playing with him, and even (mostly) fathering him.

One of the things that made me realize how much children benefit from a strong community was reading The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff. While this is her interpretation of the Ye'kuana people and she may be idealizing them a bit, it does show some important aspects of raising children that can be mimicked to a degree by a nuclear household, but would be so much better with a village. These include carrying babies, having a multi-generational group of people surrounding the child, involving children in activities, and not having an exhausted parent be the child's only social contact.

community-s8b/u4.input:
Experiments where children sleep and live apart from their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that communal sleeping eventually ended, through a mix of developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. High-quality group care, and several loving adults, can be good for children. Replacing a secure attachment to the parents is a different matter.

Tamera's Children's Place deserves to be studied directly, not caricatured. My own bias is still toward systems that widen a child's circle without making the bond between parent and child ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8b/u4.A:
But as should always be the case in experimenting with having kids sleep and live separate from their parents, extreme caution should be used. Communities like the Israeli kibbutzim who did this in the past have gradually given up the practice due to a combination of developmental findings, parental preferences, and social changes. And while it's true that kids benefit from high-quality group care and having several people who love them, nothing's ever been found that suggests that it can replace a secure attachment to parents.

Still, if somebody wants to do a study on the Tamera Children's Place, that'd be pretty interesting. Though, as always, read with the caveat that there's no hiding the fact that in these matters, there's a bias in favor of systems that don't view parents as anything but another part of the expanding circle of a kid's life, rather than as something to be avoided for ideological reasons.
community-s8b/u4.B:
Such experiments should be undertaken with extreme caution. It's been found on the Israeli Kibbutzim that communal sleeping arrengeents for children eventually are discontinued, due to a combination of findings from developmental studies, parents' prefernce, and other social changes. While it's true that children can benefit from high-quality group care (and would generally benefit from being surrounded by several different loving adults), this is no replacement for secure attachment to parent(s).

It would be very interesting to look more closely at the Children's Place at Tamera, though. (But still, like it or not, there's something inside of myself that's biased toward systems that expand the "circle of family" without making it ideologically inconvenient for parents to have a close relationship with their children.)

community-s8b/u5.input:
Children also need some territory that belongs to them. Places where they can build their own society of children, make up games, sort out ordinary disputes, and get some freedom from constant adult management.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it's still one of the freest memories I have. ZEGG's Kinderhaus works from a similar idea. The adults hold the outer safety, and the children still get a world of their own.
community-s8b/u5.A:
But even if they are not free to an extent that adults are, they should get some space to build a kind of "society of children" in which they play and resolve their problems.

One of the most free times in my life, in which I remember being really free, was actually when I was at a youth camp organized by the Unitarians. Some ideas about a children's world are also in place at ZEGG's Kinderhaus, where the adults hold the outside for the children safe, but let them have their own world.
community-s8b/u5.B:
The children also need their own places. A place where they can build their own society, play, solve problems etc. There they can be free from the adults (but still be protected by them).

I remember from my youth that the youth camp of the Unitarian Church was one of the freest things I ever experienced. This is also one of the ideas the Kinderhaus in ZEGG lives. The adults are outside and give security, inside is the world of the children.

community-s8b/u6.input:
This can be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards have to be spelled out. A children's territory can't turn into a place where adults stop paying attention. Or where older kids dominate younger ones without anyone noticing. Or where secrecy gets treated as independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats every warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. Children do well with lots of adults around who know them and enjoy them, who notice when something changes, and who will act when something's wrong. Fear can destroy that gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8b/u6.A:
Because I can see how this could be badly misunderstood, let me put some safeguards on the idea. I am not talking about leaving kids alone in their territory with no adult supervision. I am not talking about allowing older kids to dominate the territory and run the younger ones out. I am not talking about secrecy.

Also, I have to say again that I’m not buying the paranoia that seems to infect suburban communities these days, the notion that any kid who has a good relationship with an adult who is not a relative must be being abused. Kids need to have lots of adults in their lives who like them and will be alert to problems. Fear is not helpful.
community-s8b/u6.B:
Because I know this can be misunderstood, there are a few safeguards involved in allowing a territory for kids: It can’t be a place where adults stop paying attention. It can’t be a place where older kids can dominate younger kids without the adults noticing. It can’t be a place where secrecy is encouraged as a sign of independence.

And another point: I’m not talking about some kind of suburban fear where any positive connection a kid has to an adult who isn’t his parent is seen as suspect. Kids need lots of loving adults. But those adults need to be watchful, too, and ready to act if there is a problem. Let’s not allow fear to destroy what can be a wonderful thing.

community-s8b/u7.input:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. Their “no” matters. No adult is entitled to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond what legitimate safety requires, or private access.

Make a no-secrets rule. No adult asks a child to hide a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation, or a relationship from the child's mother or another trusted adult. A surprise has a date when it ends. Secrets meant to isolate the child are forbidden.
community-s8b/u7.A:
Some of these protections are:

Give a child power. Teach him/her that no adult is entitled to his or her affection, physical contact, obedience (beyond what is necessary to ensure his or her safety in a legitimate context), or access.

Have a no secret policy. No adult is allowed to ask a child to keep a secret from his or her mother or other trusted adult. No adult is allowed to give a child a secret gift, play a secret game, engage in secret physical contact, secret conversations, or secret relationships with a child.
community-s8b/u7.B:
These are some parts of it:

Kids are empowered. Kids are allowed to say no to people. It’s not okay for an adult to expect that a kid wants to hug or touch them, or do what they say (outside of legitimate safety issues), or spend time with them.

No secrets are allowed. An adult is not allowed to tell a kid that they can’t tell their mom (or whoever the kid’s trusted adults are) about a gift, a game they play, touching, what they talk about, etc.

community-s8b/u8.input:
Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Children should understand that their words carry power, and that adults will take them seriously. That teaching must never turn into interrogation, into punishing a child for being unsure, or into a reason to dismiss what a child reports. A scared or confused child may tell the story imperfectly and still need protecting.

Hear the child even when the accused person is someone people love. This is where communities fail, because that adult may be charismatic, useful, wealthy, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Decide how you'll respond before anyone's face is attached to it. Immediate safety comes first. The investigation has to be competent and fair. And nobody's status buys silence.
community-s8b/u8.A:
So you have to teach your kids to be truthful, and to know that their words have power, and will be taken seriously, without them being taught in any way by your reaction to their telling the truth that they will be punished for not being sure, or not telling it well, or that it just won't be true and they can be dismissed, when they need to be protected.

You have to be ready to listen to your kids even when the person they are accusing is loved by others in the community, often charismatic, valued, rich, important or just a good friend. You have to know what you are going to do ahead of time. First of all to make sure everyone is safe, then to make sure that it is investigated competently and fairly, and that it won't just be hushed up because the alleged offender is important.
community-s8b/u8.B:
Never get to that point. Teach your children to be truthful, and the power of their words, and that you will listen. Don't make them afraid to say anything in case they get in trouble for being wrong. Don't trivialise their words.

And you have to be prepared to listen even if they say it about someone you love. That's where many communities fail. There will be a really nice person - charismatic, helpful, rich, spiritual, a good friend - so you have to know in advance what you're going to do when you hear the news. Get the child safe immediately. Get a good investigation done - and make it fair. And don't cover it up.

community-s8b/u9.input: Keep relationships, and a way to report, outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give children perspective, and somewhere to speak. At least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route should be reachable without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, and the court gave them back after it rejected the state's blanket request. State intervention can fail spectacularly. A community that closes itself off completely can fail too. Children need more than one world.
community-s8b/u9.A: It might be a good idea to allow relationships outside the community (to grandparents, cousins, other local people, etc.) for this reason. There needs to be at least one trusted adult / advocate / reporting avenue outside the community and outside the chain of command of the community leadership. State intervention is not a reliable solution - in 1984 the state of Vermont seized 112 children in a raid at Island Pond but a court ruled that the state's blanket request for the children should be rejected and gave them back.
community-s8b/u9.B: It is wise to keep relationships and lines of reporting open outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, friends in the surrounding community, teachers and other trusted adults can be useful in giving children perspective and providing lines of reporting. At least one trusted adult, advocate and line of reporting should be available outside the community leadership. In 1984 state authorities in Vermont seized 112 children in what has been referred to as the Island Pond raid, but a court ruled against the state's blanket request for the children.

community-s8b/u10.input: I also searched the research corpus for a well-documented case, in an intentional community, of a child who stayed seriously dangerous to other people, where the record follows the whole sequence: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened afterwards. I didn't find one. That may be because the records are private, or because cases were sent elsewhere. But it means I can't claim that communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
community-s8b/u10.A: In a quick scan of my corpus of research, I couldn't find any case I had detailed notes on, in an intentional community, where a child remained very dangerous to others and where I had details on the whole sequence of assessment, intervention, and review. It may be that those cases were handled privately or relocated somewhere else, but either way it seems like there needs to be access to competent help and review outside the control of the home community.
community-s8b/u10.B: It's also the case that, despite trawling through the corpus of research data I have on this subject, I cannot find an example from any kind of intentional community of a decision to live together being tested by the presence of a child who is, to use the weakest possible form of words, seriously dangerous to other people, where the full sequence of events, assessment, intervention and review, and outcome are available for public consumption. There may well be such examples, but they are dealt with in private or by sending the case elsewhere; but in any case, it would be foolish to claim that this is a problem which communities have already solved. The child, and by extension the family and any others who might be at risk, must have the right of access to competent help and review which is not under the control of the home community.

community-s8b/u11.input:
Amish young people make an adult choice about whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. The popular caricature of Rumspringa as a free-for-all that every teenager goes through is exaggerated. But adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If a community's children never leave, it can't know whether they'd come back freely. Let them study, travel and make friends. Let them run into other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8b/u11.A:
First off, the Amish do allow their youth to choose not to become part of the church when they become adults. It is true that 85% or more do choose to join, and the Rumspringa is certainly blown out of proportion, but it is important that they are not joined until they are adults.

If the kids never leave, how can one know they would still want to come back? Let them study and travel and make friends. Let them realize that to disagree with the founders is not to be a traitor.
community-s8b/u11.B:
First off, it's a choice. The Amish let their young people make the choice to join the church when they are adults. While the Rumspringa isn't as big of a free-for-all as popular culture has portrayed, the fact that 85%, maybe even more, of the Amish youth choose to join the church shows that the majority like the way they live. The adult baptism is very important.

If the children never leave, how will they know if they want to come back? Let them learn and travel and make friends. Let them see what it's like to not agree with the founders of the community.

community-s8b/u12.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary families don't hand an eighteen-year-old a pile of money to go explore the world. They try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8b/u12.A: Just think, when someone has grown up in a community, where theres no money, or less money then what would they spend it on? They wouldnt probably spend it on travelling around the world. Most people, even from an ordinary community, wouldnt give their 18 year old child money to travel around the world, they would want them to be prepared for the next step of their life. Even more so, for those that do n't have any money, they would spend it on necessities, such as food, medical care and things that they need to survive.
community-s8b/u12.B: `` No, that's not how it works. First of all, if they're from a normal background, they wouldn't give an 18 year old a bunch of money to go travel the world. Most people try to prepare for a job or college. And if they're from a poor, money-less community, money is usually spent on more important things like food, medical care, etc.''

community-s8b/u13.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. If children grow up without using money, they especially need to know enough about the money world outside not to be helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, transportation, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next path, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can offer temporary housing, help with travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. If it can't, it can still avoid punishing anyone for leaving, or holding back the knowledge and the records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8b/u13.A: Well, if the bar is set to realistic then it's simply not making it impossibly hard for children to leave. For children who are growing up without using money it's critical that they be given the education necessary to survive in the money world, and that includes knowing how to get a job, pay rent, sign a contract, open a bank account, avoid scams, get ID, use transportation, ask for help when needed, etc. They also need to be given the skills and education they'll need to succeed once they're out, helped to make friends outside the community, have access to their records, and be given at least one option for their next step. The community can also help by providing temporary housing/transportation/tools/etc while they get set up. But if the community can't help them, they can at least not make it harder for them by not punishing them for leaving or by withholding needed information or records. Freedom isn't very meaningful if it's subject to extreme path dependency.
community-s8b/u13.B: The realistically attainable version of this standard just says that it's not okay to make it impossible for kids to leave when they grow up. This is especially important for communities that don't use money, because the kids need to know about the money world in case they want to leave. In general, it's good to try to make sure that kids have the skills, education, contacts, and documents to be able to leave the community, as well as at least one place to go. It's also helpful if the community can provide some financial assistance to help people get started, but if it can't, it should at least not make things worse by not helping them gain the necessary skills and records. No, there's no way to avoid path dependence, but there are ways of not being worse than the typical amount of path dependence.

community-s8b/u14.input:
Some of them may leave for good. Others may start communities with different values, instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty childhoods.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once a child is already living inside the disagreement. A community needs enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room left for parents to still be parents.
community-s8b/u14.A:
There’s a chance, a very real chance, that some of these people will leave. That they’ll decide to form their own communities, to work for the kind of world they want to see, rather than waiting for their kids or their kid’s kids to inherit it. To some parents, that may seem like a loss.

Couples that share a home, a culture, and a bed split apart over things like phone/screen use, vaccines, school, religion, diet, discipline, and medical care. Imagine trying to find consensus on all of those things amongst 20 different adults who all come from different backgrounds.

Good will only gets a community so far when it comes to kids. A tight band of common principles is needed, while still allowing room for parental freedom.
community-s8b/u14.B:
It’s possible that a significant portion of them will leave. It’s also possible that some of them may form their own communities with different values. From the parents’ perspective, both of these outcomes may feel like losses, but they’re actually part of the process of a movement evolving.

People who share a house, a culture, and a bed have disagreements over TV and vaccination schedules and schooling and religion and food and discipline and medical care. Just imagine a group of twenty adults, each with a different upbringing.

While it’s valuable for all the parents to have good will toward each other, it’s not enough. There needs to be enough shared principles to provide coherence in how the kids are raised, as well as enough freedom to allow parents to be parents.
